composition: The alloy is a medium-Mn, low-density δ-TRIP steel with nominal composition Fe–9Mn–5Al–0.3C (wt.%). The analysed chemical composition (Table 1, wt.%) is C 0.29, Al 4.6, Mn 8.9, P < 0.005, S < 0.005, Fe balance, i.e. the measured composition of the same heat designated Fe–9Mn–5Al–0.3C. Aluminium provides the density reduction (about a 1.3 % density decrease per 1 wt% Al) and expands the δ-ferrite phase field, so the steel cannot be fully austenitized; Mn is added as an austenite stabilizer to compensate the ferrite-forming effect of Al. The very low P and S levels reflect impurity-controlled vacuum-induction melting. The measured density of the steel is 7.34 g·cm⁻³ (Archimedes/drainage method), 6.7 % lower than that of low-carbon low-alloyed steels.
conclusions: IQ-1050 is the intercritically quenched (1050 °C/1 h + water quench) state of the Fe–9Mn–5Al–0.3C low-density δ-TRIP steel plate and functions as the parent state of the quenching–annealing (QA) study. Intercritical quenching preserves the micro-laminated δ-ferrite + lath martensite banding inherited from hot rolling but coarsens prior austenite grains, thins/segments the δ-ferrite bands, enlarges the martensite region and leaves only ~7 % retained austenite. In the processing–property sequence of the paper it marks a clear trade-off: compared with the hot-rolled parent HR it raises yield strength (305 → 575 MPa) but lowers tensile strength (1107 → 929 MPa) and gives the worst ductility of all conditions (2.0 % total elongation, 1.9 GPa% PSE). Its poor ductility and low retained-austenite content are the motivation for the subsequent 1 h anneals at 620–800 °C, which restore 40–63 % elongation and PSE above 30 GPa% (best at QA-740, 45.2 GPa%). The experimental steel after the full quenching–annealing route offers a wide yield-strength grade (460–620 MPa) with excellent ductility and low yield-to-tensile ratio, and is proposed as a low-density candidate for high-strength automobile steel plate, substituting for TRIP 590T/400Y (SAE J2745-2007).
mechanisms: Holding the hot-rolled steel at 1050 °C reverses all martensite back into austenite; diffusion of C and Mn into the austenite increases the austenite volume fraction, which in turn produces a larger lath martensite fraction at room temperature.

The high reheating temperature of 1050 °C lowers the Mn content of the reversed austenite, decreasing austenite stability and raising the Ms temperature; the higher cooling rate of water quenching than air cooling further inhibits α-ferrite transformation and also raises Ms, so the martensite region of IQ-1050 is larger and its retained austenite is fewer than in HR.

Because prior austenite grains grow during the 1050 °C hold and their boundaries (PAGB) move into the δ-ferrite, the δ-ferrite bands are thinned and even split into discontinuous δ-ferrite grains — explaining the segmented, dispersed ferrite bands of IQ-1050.

Heating to 1050 °C largely decreases the GND density of the hot-rolled microstructure, but the considerable martensitic transformation during quenching causes volume expansion, so the lath martensite and retained austenite of IQ-1050 still retain high GND densities (8.23 × 10¹⁴ m⁻² BCC, 5.01 × 10¹⁴ m⁻² FCC).

The larger amount of lath martensite in IQ-1050 relative to HR raises the yield strength (to 575 ± 13 MPa) and the higher block-boundary density produced by quenching also contributes to this yield-strength increase.

The same martensite-rich microstructure is prone to stress concentration during deformation, causing premature failure; this is why IQ-1050 shows a poorer tensile strength (929 ± 30 MPa) and very poor ductility (2.0 ± 0.3 %) despite its higher yield strength.

The intercritically quenched state is mechanically unstable in tension: its limited retained austenite (~7 %) provides little TRIP contribution, so IQ-1050 does not benefit from the transformation-induced plasticity that raises the ductility of the subsequently annealed QA specimens.
microstructure: IQ-1050 keeps the micro-laminated (banded) microstructure of the hot-rolled state through heredity, consisting of alternating δ-ferrite bands and a lath martensite region (three phases: δ-ferrite, lath martensite, retained austenite). During the 1 h hold at 1050 °C all the martensite in the hot-rolled steel reversed into austenite, prior austenite grains grew, and the prior austenite grain boundaries (PAGB) moved into the δ-ferrite, so the δ-ferrite bands became thinner and were even divided into some discontinuous δ-ferrite grains by the prior austenite (clearly seen in SEM and EBSD band-contrast maps). The δ-ferrite (BCC, A2) band regions after 1050 °C holding are therefore thinner, segmented and dispersed; the lath martensite region is larger than in HR, and retained austenite (FCC) is the scarcest among all conditions, present only as small isolated patches with an EBSD volume fraction of ~7 % (XRD value not measured for this sample). Prior austenite grain boundaries that moved to the δ-ferrite are visible in the microstructure. Geometrically necessary dislocation (GND) densities calculated from EBSD KAM data are 8.23 × 10¹⁴ m⁻² for the BCC phase (ferrite plus martensite) and 5.01 × 10¹⁴ m⁻² for the FCC phase — lower than HR (10.81 and 8.37 × 10¹⁴ m⁻², respectively) but still high because considerable martensitic transformation during quenching caused volume expansion. In the grain-boundary statistics, the block-boundary (> 45°) density of IQ-1050 is higher than its austenitic-grain (AG) boundary density, an inversion relative to HR, indicating that more austenite underwent martensitic transformation than in HR. No carbides are reported in IQ-1050 (carbides appear only in QA-620).
processing: The processing path is: (1) vacuum-induction melting of a 5 kg ingot; (2) homogenization at 1100 °C for 2 h; (3) forging into a square forging ingot of 80 mm × 70 mm; (4) reheating to 1100 °C and holding 2 h; (5) hot rolling from 80 to 12 mm thickness in eight passes, with an initial rolling temperature of about 1050 °C and a finishing rolling temperature of about 950 °C (thermomechanical rolling in the dual-phase region produced the micro-laminated δ-ferrite/martensite structure); (6) air cooling to room temperature, giving the hot-rolled parent state labeled HR. IQ-1050 itself is then produced by (7) intercritical reheating of the hot-rolled plate to 1050 °C, in the ferrite + austenite dual-phase region, for 1 h, followed by (8) water quenching. The 1050 °C quenching temperature was chosen because the equilibrium austenite fraction reaches a maximum of about 91.4 % near 970 °C; allowing for the discrepancy of the Thermo-Calc calculation, 1050 °C was selected to make the austenite volume large enough. Water quenching gives a higher cooling rate than the air cooling used for HR. This intercritically quenched state is the precursor of the subsequent 1 h anneals at 620, 680, 740 and 800 °C (samples QA-620, QA-680, QA-740, QA-800).
properties: Room-temperature tensile testing (electronic tensile machine WDW-100E, strain rate 0.375 min⁻¹, rod-shaped specimen M10 × 60 mm with 25 mm gauge length, tensile axis parallel to the rolling direction of the hot-rolled plate) gives for IQ-1050: yield strength 575 ± 13 MPa, ultimate tensile strength 929 ± 30 MPa, total elongation 2.0 ± 0.3 %, yield-to-tensile ratio 0.62 and product of strength and elongation 1.9 ± 0.4 GPa%. The engineering stress–strain curve (Fig. 5a) peaks near 900 MPa at about 2 % strain. Relative to the hot-rolled parent HR (YS 305 ± 11 MPa, TS 1107 ± 32 MPa, TE 5.6 ± 0.4 %, PSE 6.2 ± 0.6 GPa%), intercritical quenching raises the yield strength appreciably but lowers the tensile strength, and IQ-1050 has the poorest total elongation of all the specimens studied. Relative to the annealed QA series, IQ-1050 has the highest strength/yield level apart from QA-620 but by far the lowest ductility. Characterization techniques applied to this sample include field-emission SEM (MIRA-3 LMH) on 10 % nital-etched specimens, EBSD (Oxford Instruments, specimens electropolished in 10 % perchloric acid + 5 % glycerol + 85 % ethanol at 15–20 V and 0.8–1.2 A, analyzed with HKL Channel5 and Python), KAM/GND analysis and grain-boundary classification, Thermo-Calc (TCFE 12) equilibrium calculations, and room-temperature tensile testing; XRD was used for the annealed QA specimens rather than for IQ-1050.
summary: IQ-1050 is the intercritically quenched state of a Fe–9Mn–5Al–0.3C (wt.%) low-density δ-TRIP steel plate. It was produced by reheating the hot-rolled plate (HR) to 1050 °C — a temperature lying in the ferrite + austenite dual-phase region — holding for 1 h and then water quenching. The sample retains the micro-laminated (banded) δ-ferrite + lath martensite microstructure inherited from hot rolling but with a larger martensite region and only ~7 % retained austenite, and it serves as the parent/intermediate state from which the quenched-and-annealed QA-620/680/740/800 series is derived in this study of annealing-temperature effects.
unmapped: The GND density of HR and IQ-1050 is comparable to values reported for strained Hadfield austenitic steel at a true strain of ~0.05, about 9.80 × 10¹⁴/m².

In the QA series derived from IQ-1050, carbides (considered cementite) precipitate widely in the tempered martensite region only at the 620 °C annealing temperature; austenite volume fractions by EBSD are ~28, ~35, ~50 and ~49 % for QA-620/680/740/800, and by XRD ~33, ~37, ~51 and ~48 %.
